segments.text: They call it the real-life money heist.
A crew took over a bank in Argentina, got the police to bring them pizza,
then vanished with hundreds of police outside.
This is the true story of the Banco Rio robbery.
The day they fooled a whole country.
Friday the 13th, 2006.
A calm man in a grey suit walked into a bank near Buenos Aires.
His name was Mario.
His crew came too, in disguise.
A fake doctor in a white coat, and a man in a blonde wig.
Another, in a blue cap, made the guard lock the front door.
Holding guns, they gathered everyone inside and sat them down.
23 people were now hostages.
Some of the robbers went down to the basement,
to the safe deposit boxes where people kept cash and jewels.
Outside, police cars kept coming, until hundreds of police ringed the bank.
TV cameras went live, and all of Argentina watched the front door.
Somewhere, one of these men had a wife.
Remember her?
A police negotiator got Mario on the phone, and they talked for hours.
Mario was calm, even friendly.
He said there were nine of them inside, too many to rush.
It was a bluff, there were fewer.
He asked for food, bring me some pizzas and soft drinks, and the police sent them in.
Every minute he talked, gave his crew more time to empty the boxes.
One slip, and the police would storm in.
One hostage, a lawyer, had her birthday that day.
So the robbers sang her happy birthday.
But for the hostages, it was a frightening day, and some needed help long after.
Downstairs, the crew opened box after box, and behind a tall cabinet,
cold air blew up from below.
Then Mario stopped answering.
The police waited, and the special unit got ready.
After seven in the evening, the special unit stormed in.
They found the hostages alive, and the boxes broken open.
But the robbers were gone.
Hundreds of police had watched that bank all day.
So how did they get out?
If you had been the negotiator, would you have believed Mario?
Part two is next.
How they vanished, and the note they left behind.
